newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Communists could control Russian budget's fate.
newsitem.headline: Communists could control Russian budget's fate.

text.p: Russia's draft budget, to be debated by the State Duma lower house of parliament on Sunday, must pass through three Duma readings and win the upper house's approval before President Boris Yeltsin can sign it into law.
At least half the Duma's 450 members must vote for the budget for it to pass.
Observers say the budget's fate will depend largely on which way the well-disciplined communist faction votes, and partly on whether the Duma decides to hold a secret ballot or an open one.
Government plans are often approved during secret ballots.
Here is an outline of the main groups in the Duma, and the way they could vote on Sunday.
COMMUNIST PARTY OF THE RUSSIAN FEDERATION (KPRF), headed by Gennady Zyuganov, is the biggest Duma faction with 147 seats and the government's main opponent.

The communists in principle oppose the government budget, but some party deputies have said the party may vote for the 1997 budget if the government works out a longer-term economic plan to tackle social issues.
The Duma's main pro-government group, OUR HOME IS RUSSIA, has 65 seats in the Duma and is headed by Sergei Belyayev. It will vote for the budget.

The LIBERAL-DEMOCRATIC PARTY OF RUSSIA (LDPR) has 51 deputies and is headed by flamboyant ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky, who unexpectedly supported the budget in last week's parliamentary debate.
In an abrupt shift of policy, Zhirinovsky said the Duma had to pass the budget to control government financial policies.

YABLOKO, Russia's main liberal party with 46 representatives in the Duma, has decided to vote against the draft. Its leader, economist Grigory Yavlinsky, said the plan gave too high a figure for income, while spending was too low to be true.

Yabloko has said it will only change its mind if the government meets certain conditions, including amending tax legislation and publishing a list of state-owned property. The government has indicated that the conditions are not acceptable.
The RUSSIAN REGIONS GROUP, whose 42 deputies mostly represent the interests of regional adminstrations and businesses, is likely to be divided in the budget vote.
Deputies from rich Russian regions are likely to support the budget, those from poor ones to reject it.
The AGRARIAN PARTY has 37 deputies representing interests of Soviet-era collective farms and is likely to follow the communist line.
The 37 nationalist and communist deputies of the NARODOVLASTIYE (PEOPLE'S POWER) group are also likely to vote the same way as the communists.
There are also some 25 independent deputies. Some will vote for the budget, some will oppose it.
